native_result.query: What kind of demographic disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated?
native_result.HypoA: Gender disparities exist in median wealth in 1985 among individuals who were ever incarcerated, with males having higher median wealth than females.
native_result.HypoB: Among the 289 ever-incarcerated (1985-1994) NLS-Y79 respondents, 1985 wealth disparities track RACE rather than SEX, and take the form of a white vs non-white gap: hispanic (original label 'hipanic', henceforth hispanic) and black respondents are statistically indistinguishable (median $320 vs $0; difference $320, 95% CI -1,441 to 1,480, p=0.58), while whites hold $2,200 (white-black difference $1,880, CI -100 to 5,000; white-hispanic $2,200, CI -400 to 5,000; Mann-Whitney p=0.046 and 0.041), with 31.9% of whites versus 47.8% of blacks and 52.5% of hispanics holding zero-or-negative net wealth (17.2 pp gap for pooled non-white vs white, 95% CI 3.9-29.8 pp). The racial disadvantage persists within men: white men $2,000 vs black men $800 (0.40x, 14.2 pp more at <=0) and hispanic men $700 (0.35x, 16.3 pp more at <=0), although within-male median differences alone are not significant (p=0.15, 0.19). By contrast, the apparent sex gap (men $1,000 vs women $0; 29.0 pp more women at <=0) cannot be asserted as an independent disparity because all 37 ever-incarcerated women fall into cells of n=12/16/9 and the direction reverses among white women (median $4,100, the highest of the six race-by-sex cells). Race and sex each explain only ~1.8% of rank variation (race x sex 5.0%), so the dominant pattern is a shared floor of asset poverty - Q1=$0 in every cell and 45.0% of ever-incarcerated respondents at <=0 net wealth, versus 31.8% and a $3,600 median among the never-incarcerated - overlaid by a racial gradient that is modest in dollars ($1,200-2,200) but 3-7x in ratio and consistent across medians, winsorized means and shares at or below zero. Because ever_jailed covers 1985-1994 while wealth is measured in 1985, this disparity is best read as an associative, largely pre-existing economic disadvantage shaping who becomes incarcerated rather than a causal effect of incarceration; the data contain no residence/institution ('Jail') fields to verify incarceration status independently, and $100 value granularity plus 1,899 exact duplicate rows add only about +/- $50 of noise (jitter check), an order of magnitude below the estimated gaps. Contextually, the gap widens after the incarceration window (ever-incarcerated medians $0 in 1990 and 1996 vs $10,500 and $8,500 for the never-incarcerated), and by 1996 the internal racial gap collapses to $0 at the median because both groups hit the zero floor.
native_result.WorkflowB: 1) Loaded data/nls_incarceration_processed.csv (12,013 x 6; 0 missing; 1,899 exact duplicates) and subset ever_jailed==1 (n=289). 2) For the overall group, by race, by sex and by race x sex computed n, median, Q1, Q3, % with wealth <=0, raw mean and 99% winsorized mean (global caps: 1st pct -$5,063, 99th pct $273,949) with 95% percentile bootstrap CIs for every median (5,000 resamples, seed 20261022). 3) Crossed cells compared against the single white-male reference: dollar difference with bootstrap CI of the difference, difference in % with wealth <=0, and median ratio (ratios omitted whenever the reference median is <=0); cells with n<20 flagged as descriptive/non-conclusive. 4) Full pairwise matrices for the margins (white/black/hipanic; male/female) with bootstrap CIs of differences and Mann-Whitney tests. 5) Axis ranking: spread of marginal medians (race $2,200 vs sex $1,000), race gaps within men and within women, sex gap within each race (sign flips), rank-based eta-squared (race 0.0185, sex 0.0178, race x sex 0.0500), Kruskal tests, pooled white vs non-white comparison and probability-of-superiority effect size robust to ties. 6) Context table comparing ever-incarcerated with never-incarcerated overall, by sex and by race x sex. 7) Sensitivity: uniform +/- $50 jitter for $100 granularity (2,000 replicates), duplicate-rows check with an explicit note that deduplication changes the estimand, and composite_wealth_1990/1996 used only as brief contextual robustness. Outputs: out/table_main.csv, out/table_race_sex_vs_whitemale.csv, out/pairwise_race.csv, out/pairwise_sex.csv, out/context_vs_neverincarcerated.csv, out/sensitivity.csv, out/diagnostics.json, out/extra_diagnostics.json.

sub_hypo.context: Male NLS-Y79 respondents with ever_jailed=1; 1985 wealth, using white men as the reference.

sub_hypo.context: NLS-Y79 respondents compared by incarceration during 1985–1994, with baseline wealth measured in 1985; no residence or institution ('Jail') fields are available to independently verify incarceration status.

sub_hypo.context: NLS-Y79 respondents with ever_jailed=1, comparing whites with pooled black and Hispanic respondents in 1996.
sub_hypo.relations: Both groups have median wealth of $0, yielding a $0 white versus non-white median difference.

sub_hypo.text: The estimated baseline wealth disparities are substantially larger than the noise associated with the recorded wealth granularity in the sensitivity checks.
